paragraphs.heading: What a press does
paragraphs.text: A printing press is a machine that pushes ink onto paper, cloth or something similar by applying pressure. Before it, printers rubbed the paper by hand to pick up the ink, so the press was a big step forward. The German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg invented it around 1440.

paragraphs.heading: Why the time was right
paragraphs.text: Late medieval Europe was ready for such a machine. Trade was growing, and so was the urban middle class, while new universities kept raising the demand for books. Copying books by hand was slow and costly. By the 1400s there were far fewer manuscripts than people wanted.

paragraphs.heading: Four old ideas, one new system
paragraphs.text: Gutenberg did not start from nothing. He brought together four things that already existed: movable type, the screw press, paper made by machine, and the codex book format. The screw press, used by farmers to squeeze grapes and olives, let pressure be applied straight down onto a flat surface. Movable type means building a text out of separate letters that can be reused. To these Gutenberg added his own inventions, such as an ink based on oil that suited metal letters, and a hand-held mold for casting the type.

paragraphs.heading: Earlier type in East Asia
paragraphs.text: Movable type was older than Gutenberg. In the 11th century the Chinese artisan Bi Sheng made type from baked clay, and the oldest surviving book printed with metal type is the Korean Jikji of 1377. None of these methods spread widely, though, and woodblock printing remained the main method in East Asia. Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters, which made a full set of type expensive, whereas the Latin alphabet needs only a small set.

paragraphs.heading: What printing changed
paragraphs.text: Printing opened an age of mass communication in Europe. Information spread quickly across the continent, feeding the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution. Printed texts became cheaper and easier to find, which helped more adults learn to read. More books appeared in local languages instead of Latin, and national languages became standardized.

paragraphs.heading: From wood to steam
paragraphs.text: The wooden hand press barely changed for more than three hundred years. Then came an iron press, and later presses driven by steam power and rotary motion. Hoe's rotary press of 1843 raised output sharply, and later rotary machines could make millions of page impressions a day.
